Pricing by simulation¶

Back to Monte Carlo

The Monte Carlo price of a European option is the average of the discounted payoff over simulated paths. Each model has a function with the same signature as its semi-analytic pricers:

double prc::heston_price_mc(type, spot, strike, rate, dividend_yield, maturity, const vol::HestonParams &, const prc::MonteCarloOptions & = {}, Config = {});
// the same for bates_price_mc, sv_price_mc, heston_nandi_price_mc, sabr_price_mc (forward in place of spot), slv_price_mc, rough_heston_price_mc, rough_bergomi_price_mc
struct prc::MonteCarloOptions {
  std::int64_t paths = 40000, steps = 252;
  vol::SimScheme scheme = Euler;  vol::RandMethod rand_method = Pseudo;  bool randomized_quasi = false;  int sobol_scrambling = 0;
  bool antithetic = false, control_variate = false, importance_sampling = false;  double importance_shift = 0.0, control_vol = 0.0;
  std::uint64_t offset = 0, seed = 0;
};

The simulation is risk neutral: the drift is set to rate − dividend_yield whatever mu the parameter struct holds. A maturity of zero returns the intrinsic value. The result is a single number, with no error bar; its uncertainty is found by repeating the price with different seeds.

The error falls as 1/√N¶

The statistical error of a Monte Carlo price is σ/√N, with σ the standard deviation of one discounted payoff. The program prices a Heston call 12 times with different seeds at each number of paths, and prints the mean, the standard deviation of the 12 prices (the standard error of one run) and that standard deviation times √N, which should be roughly constant. The COS price is the reference.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace prc = pluss::subsp::math::finance::pricing;
namespace vol = pluss::subsp::math::finance::volatility;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(4));
  const double spot = 100.0, strike = 100.0, rate = 0.03, dividend = 0.01, maturity = 1.0;
  const vol::HestonParams params;
  const double reference = prc::heston_price_cos(prc::Call, spot, strike, rate, dividend, maturity, params);
  out.writeln("COS reference", reference);
  out.writeln("   paths     mean of 12     std dev of one run    std dev x sqrt(paths)");
  for (std::int64_t paths : {1000, 4000, 16000, 64000}) {
    std::vector<double> prices;
    for (int seed = 1; seed <= 12; ++seed) {
      prc::MonteCarloOptions options;
      options.paths = paths;
      options.steps = 32;
      options.seed = 100 + seed;
      prices.push_back(prc::heston_price_mc(prc::Call, spot, strike, rate, dividend, maturity, params, options));
    }
    double mean = 0.0;
    for (double p : prices) {
      mean += p / 12.0;
    }
    double variance = 0.0;
    for (double p : prices) {
      variance += (p - mean) * (p - mean) / 11.0;
    }
    out.writeln(paths, mean, std::sqrt(variance), std::sqrt(variance) * std::sqrt(static_cast<double>(paths)));
  }
}

Output

COS reference 8.5423
   paths     mean of 12     std dev of one run    std dev x sqrt(paths)
1000 8.5427 0.4135 13.0768
4000 8.4464 0.1361 8.6058
16000 8.5430 0.0609 7.7094
64000 8.5694 0.0355 8.9810

The standard deviation of one run falls from 0.41 at 1000 paths to 0.036 at 64000, and its product with √paths stays in the same range (13.1, 8.6, 7.7 and 9.0; each standard deviation is itself estimated from 12 runs, so it carries an error of about 20%). The means of 12 runs are within 0.1 of the reference at every size. Quadrupling the number of paths roughly halves the error, as it should.

The discretisation bias¶

Besides the statistical error there is a bias from replacing the continuous process by steps time steps. It falls with the number of steps but, for the same effort, takes paths away. The program prices the same call with 4 to 128 steps, with enough paths and seeds that the statistical error (printed) is small against the bias.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace prc = pluss::subsp::math::finance::pricing;
namespace vol = pluss::subsp::math::finance::volatility;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(4));
  const double spot = 100.0, strike = 100.0, rate = 0.03, dividend = 0.01, maturity = 1.0;
  const vol::HestonParams params;
  const double reference = prc::heston_price_cos(prc::Call, spot, strike, rate, dividend, maturity, params);
  out.writeln("COS reference", reference);
  out.writeln("   steps     mean of 8 runs     bias      standard error of the mean");
  for (std::int64_t steps : {4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}) {
    std::vector<double> prices;
    for (int seed = 1; seed <= 8; ++seed) {
      prc::MonteCarloOptions options;
      options.paths = 30000;
      options.steps = steps;
      options.seed = 500 + seed;
      prices.push_back(prc::heston_price_mc(prc::Call, spot, strike, rate, dividend, maturity, params, options));
    }
    double mean = 0.0;
    for (double p : prices) {
      mean += p / 8.0;
    }
    double variance = 0.0;
    for (double p : prices) {
      variance += (p - mean) * (p - mean) / 7.0;
    }
    out.writeln(steps, mean, mean - reference, std::sqrt(variance / 8.0));
  }
}

Output

COS reference 8.5423
   steps     mean of 8 runs     bias      standard error of the mean
4 8.7362 0.1939 0.0211
8 8.6700 0.1278 0.0230
16 8.6101 0.0679 0.0308
32 8.5528 0.0106 0.0173
64 8.5531 0.0108 0.0283
128 8.5418 -0.0004 0.0201

The bias falls with the number of steps, from +0.194 at 4 steps through +0.128, +0.068 and +0.011 at 8, 16 and 32. At 32 steps and above the bias is no longer distinguishable from the statistical error of the mean (0.017 to 0.030), which is the point of diminishing return: more steps cost proportionally more time and give nothing measurable.

Schemes¶

SimScheme selects how the variance is stepped. Euler is the simplest; Milstein and Milstein2 add a correction term; QuadExp is Andersen’s quadratic-exponential scheme, which matches the first two moments of the variance exactly and handles a variance near zero; Transition samples the exact non-central chi-squared transition of the square-root process (this needs the degree 4κθ/σ² of that distribution to exceed 1, so that the sampler can be driven by the shock that is correlated with the spot; below it, Transition uses the quadratic-exponential step instead). With 32 steps and parameters that satisfy the Feller condition they price alike; they differ when the variance is often near zero, which the next program arranges with a small mean reversion and a large volatility of variance.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace prc = pluss::subsp::math::finance::pricing;
namespace vol = pluss::subsp::math::finance::volatility;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(4));
  const double spot = 100.0, strike = 100.0, rate = 0.03, dividend = 0.01, maturity = 1.0;
  vol::HestonParams params;
  params.kappa = 0.5;
  params.theta = 0.04;
  params.sigma = 1.0;  // 2 kappa theta = 0.04 is far below sigma^2 = 1: the variance is often near zero
  params.rho = -0.7;
  const double reference = prc::heston_price_cos(prc::Call, spot, strike, rate, dividend, maturity, params);
  out.writeln("COS reference", reference);
  const std::vector<std::pair<const char *, vol::SimScheme>> schemes{{"Euler    ", vol::SimScheme::Euler}, {"Milstein ", vol::SimScheme::Milstein}, {"Milstein2", vol::SimScheme::Milstein2},
                                                                    {"QuadExp  ", vol::SimScheme::QuadExp}, {"Transition", vol::SimScheme::Transition}};
  for (const auto &[name, scheme] : schemes) {
    std::vector<double> prices;
    for (int seed = 1; seed <= 8; ++seed) {
      prc::MonteCarloOptions options;
      options.paths = 30000;
      options.steps = 32;
      options.scheme = scheme;
      options.seed = 900 + seed;
      prices.push_back(prc::heston_price_mc(prc::Call, spot, strike, rate, dividend, maturity, params, options));
    }
    double mean = 0.0;
    for (double p : prices) {
      mean += p / 8.0;
    }
    out.writeln(name, " mean of 8 runs", mean, " bias", mean - reference);
  }
}

Output

COS reference 6.1563
Euler      mean of 8 runs 8.2822  bias 2.1260
Milstein   mean of 8 runs 8.6197  bias 2.4634
Milstein2  mean of 8 runs 8.6276  bias 2.4714
QuadExp    mean of 8 runs 6.2173  bias 0.0610
Transition  mean of 8 runs 6.2173  bias 0.0610

With a variance process that violates the Feller condition badly, the schemes differ widely against the COS price of 6.1563. Euler and the two Milstein schemes are biased by more than 2 (35%) because they cannot represent a variance that sits near zero. The quadratic-exponential scheme is accurate (bias 0.061, within the statistical error). Transition gives the same result, because for these parameters its exact sampler cannot be driven by the correlated shock, so it uses the quadratic-exponential step.
